### 1. Compare the curved edges
Since the outside boundary of a square must be straight, every curved edge must be internal and must meet a complementary curved edge.

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\text{Piece} & \text{Convex} & \text{Concave}\\ \hline
A&0&2\\
B&1&1\\
C&2&0\\
D&1&0\\
E&0&1
\end{array}
\]

Only omitting \(B\) or \(D\) leaves equal numbers of convex and concave edges.

### 2. Use the straight edges
Pieces \(A,B,C\) have exactly two straight edges, which must form their two outer sides in the \(2\times2\) square.

- If \(D\) were omitted, only \(E\) would have a third straight edge available for an internal join, but there would be no second straight edge to match it. Thus \(D\) cannot be the omitted piece.
- If \(B\) is omitted, the four remaining pieces can be arranged as follows:
  - \(D\) upper-left,
  - \(A\) upper-right,
  - \(E\) lower-left,
  - \(C\) lower-right.

The internal joins are then:
- \(D\)'s convex edge with \(A\)'s concave edge,
- \(A\)'s other concave edge with \(C\)'s convex edge,
- \(C\)'s other convex edge with \(E\)'s concave edge,
- \(E\)'s straight edge with \(D\)'s straight edge.

Thus \(A,C,D,E\) form the square, so the unused piece is
